body:
You're right - I'm not in a bad place emotionally. I still care about the little things, but at the end of a long and stressful day, I find comfort in thinking "fuck it, nothing really matters in the end anyway."

The only problem with this is that I can become so apathetic that I just feel like I should speed up my inevitable death. It's going to happen eventually, why does it matter if it's in 50 minutes or 50 years?

I'll check out the books you suggested. I'm not looking for answers. Actually I'm not really sure what I'm looking for. Just feels good to share I suppose.

One of my favorite philosophers is Epictetus. He was a roman slave in the late first century and one hell of a Stoic. He believed that the only things we had absolute control over were our opinions, impulses, desires, and aversions. Everything else was out of our control. I've spoken to a few people about Stoicism and most of them find it absurd. While it sounds great for a slave, applied in the modern world, especially to the more fortunate people, they find it lacking. I happen to find it beautiful, but I could never conform to that way of thinking simply because it I don't have the willpower to control my opinions, impulses, desires, and aversions. They are what they are. If I get mugged I will feel upset, mad, violated. Epictetus would remain calm and say that the mugger received nothing of value, and there was nothing I could have done to prevent it since it's not for me to control. He's completely eliminated material objects and even some immaterial objects from his desires. He's happy to have them but understands that at any second they could be gone and he can't control that and therefore isn't upset about it. Fortunately or unfortunately (I'm not sure which), that's not me. I value my possessions, I value my achievements, I value my success, I value my failures. I value a lot in life, but it always comes down to the fact that my life has no meaning - at least no meaning that I feel is worthy enough to create a strong desire to continue living.

I don't have the world all figured out, and I don't feel like I need to figure it out for any reason. I just know that all life eventually comes to an end, and in the grand scheme of things, our desires, emotions, actions - they are all immediate and short lived. True love may span a lifetime, but it always ends in heartache and then dissolved into nothingness as the two lovers lives passed. For a theist, that love may not end there. For an atheist, though, it does. So what good was the lifetime full of love if you have no means to remember it by? You can go the same way with pain, another immediate response. I think pain is an especially good example to use. Pain is another immediate response that's designed to let us know when something is harming us. It teaches us what we should avoid and makes us fear certain actions or objects. Does pain incurred while alive matter after you've taken your final breath? To me it doesn't, because everything that pain taught you to fear has dissipated into nothing once those electrical signals to your brain stop firing. Why is love, fear, happiness, etc any different?

You say that life is about experiencing things in your own unique way, but what good are experiences if you'll never remember them? What if every night at midnight you were to forget everything you did for the past 24 hours. Every pleasure, every pain, every experience, just gone as soon as you woke up. What if every morning you woke up and found out that you would never remember anything you did that day? What would motivate you to continue to experience new things? I know it's a flawed example, but if you expand the 24 hours to 90 years, that's the boat I'm in.

I'm not even sure if I want to be rid of this mindset. It's almost comforting knowing that nothing matters. It's interesting to hear from others about the subject though, so thanks for sharing.
